items.title: Longest contiguous stretch under a distinctness or count budget
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** The candidate is handed a sequence and a budget expressed over a contiguous stretch of it — at most *k* distinct values, at most *k* replacements, no repeated value — and asked for the longest (or shortest) stretch that stays inside the budget.

The naive answer re-examines every start and end pair. The expected answer keeps two indices and a running tally of what the current stretch contains, advancing the right index to admit an element and the left index only far enough to restore the budget. Each index moves forward only, which is what turns the quadratic scan linear.

What an interviewer is actually measuring: whether the candidate can state the invariant the window maintains, and whether the shrink step is driven by that invariant instead of by a guessed condition.

items.title: Nearest larger neighbour resolved with an order-maintaining stack
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** For every position in a sequence, report something about the closest position on one side that beats it — how far away the next larger value sits, how many consecutive earlier entries it dominates, how wide a bar can extend before a shorter bar stops it.

The expected answer sweeps once, holding a stack of positions whose answer is still unsettled and whose values fall in one direction. A new element resolves and removes every stacked position it beats, so each position is pushed once and popped once and the sweep is linear.

What an interviewer is actually measuring: whether the candidate can say what the stacked entries are still waiting for, and can defend the amortised bound rather than describing the structure as merely sorted.

items.title: Minimise a maximum by bisecting the space of candidate answers
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** Nothing in the input is sorted, and the question asks for the smallest value of some ceiling that still lets a plan succeed — the smallest capacity, the lowest rate, the shortest deadline. The candidate is expected to notice that *feasible* is monotone in that ceiling: raise it and a working plan keeps working.

The answer is therefore a bisection over the range of candidate ceilings, with a cheap greedy or counting routine as the feasibility test, giving a logarithmic number of linear checks.

What an interviewer is actually measuring: whether the candidate argues monotonicity *before* writing the loop, picks bounds that are provably feasible and infeasible, and lands the boundary without an off-by-one.

items.title: Longest paint run a mixing head can produce without a purge
items.statement_md:
A paint line applies one colour to each panel as the panels roll past, and the sequence of colours for a shift is fixed in advance. The mixing head can hold at most `k` colours loaded at once. It may be loaded once, at the start of a run of consecutive panels, and must be purged before any panel needing a colour it does not hold.

Given `colors`, a list of colour codes in panel order, and the integer `k`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive panels that uses at most `k` distinct colours, so the head can carry that whole run on one loading.

Implement `longest_uniform_batch(colors, k)`.

- `colors` may be empty; colour codes are arbitrary hashable values.
- If `k` is zero or negative no panel can be served, so the answer is `0`.
- Target `O(n)` time in the number of panels.

hints: Ask what changes when one more panel joins the run on the right. Do you have to look at the whole run again to know how many distinct colours it holds?
Keep a tally of how many times each colour appears in the current run. The number of distinct colours is the size of that tally.
When the tally grows past k, drop panels from the left one at a time and decrement their counts, deleting a colour whose count reaches zero, until the tally fits again.
Both ends only ever move right, so each panel is added once and removed at most once. Record the best length after every shrink, not only at the end.
follow_ups: Return the start and end panel indices of one longest run, not just its length. Which one do you return if several tie?
Now the head may be purged up to p times in a shift. What does the problem become, and is the same two-index sweep still enough?
Colour codes arrive as a stream you cannot index backwards. What state would you need to keep to answer the same question online?

def make_input(n):

    r = random.Random(20260820)
    # Alphabet size == k, so the whole run is one legal window and a naive
    # per-start rescan degenerates to O(n^2). A wider alphabet hides it.
    return [[r.randrange(4) for _ in range(n)], 4]

items.title: How long a pressure reading has stood unbeaten on a well log
items.statement_md:
A downhole gauge writes one pressure reading per hour, oldest first. For a report, each hour needs its **standing span**: the number of consecutive hours ending at that hour, and running backwards, whose readings are all less than or equal to that hour's reading. The hour itself always counts, so every span is at least `1`, and the span stops at the first earlier hour that reads strictly higher.

Given `readings`, a list of integers in chronological order, return a list of the same length holding each hour's standing span.

Implement `pressure_spans(readings)`.

- Readings may repeat, and may be negative.
- An empty log returns an empty list.
- Aim for `O(n)` total time; a per-hour backward scan is the answer to beat.

hints: Write the brute force first and say out loud what work it repeats when readings rise steadily.
An hour whose reading is beaten by a later hour can never end anybody's span again. Once you have used it, it is dead.
Hold a stack of hour indices whose readings strictly decrease. For a new hour, pop while the stacked reading is less than or equal to the new one.
After popping, if the stack is empty every earlier hour was beaten, so the span is index+1; otherwise it is the gap to the index now on top. Then push the new hour.
follow_ups: The report changes so that a span stops at an earlier hour reading greater than *or equal to* the current one. What single character moves, and why?
Readings arrive live and you must emit each span as it arrives. Does your solution already work, and what is the worst-case memory?
Prove the linear bound to me. How many times can one index be pushed and popped?

    return [list(range(n))]

items.title: Split a fixed job queue across shifts to flatten the busiest one
items.statement_md:
A batch plant has a queue of jobs that must run in the order given; reordering them would break their data dependencies. The queue is cut into at most `workers` contiguous blocks, and each block runs on one worker. A worker's load is the sum of the durations in its block, and the plant's shift length is set by the **busiest** worker.

Given `jobs`, a list of non-negative integer durations, and the integer `workers`, return the smallest possible busiest-worker load over all ways of cutting the queue into at most `workers` contiguous blocks.

Implement `min_peak_load(jobs, workers)`.

- An empty queue costs `0`, whatever `workers` is.
- With a non-empty queue and `workers <= 0` nothing can run: return `-1`.
- `workers` may exceed the number of jobs; blocks may not be empty in that case, so surplus workers simply idle.
- Aim for `O(n log S)` where `S` is the total duration.

items.title: Longest certifiable stretch of a bottling run
items.statement_md:
A bottling line records one check per bottle as it leaves the filler: `0` when the fill was
within spec and `1` when it was not.

Quality will certify a **contiguous** stretch of the run as sellable provided it holds **at
most `k`** out-of-spec bottles — those get pulled by hand afterwards, and past `k` of them
that stops being worth doing.

Given the checks in the order they were recorded and the budget `k`, return the length of
the longest stretch that can be certified.

`checks` holds only `0` and `1` and may be empty; `k` is zero or more. A `k` of zero means a
certified stretch may hold no failures at all. Return `0` when nothing qualifies.

hints: Extend a stretch by one bottle on the right. What happens to the number of failures inside it, and do you have to look at the rest of the stretch to know?
Carry one running count of the failures inside the current stretch. Adding a bottle on the right adds its check to that count, and that is the whole update.
When the count goes above k, move the left end right — subtracting each check you drop — until it is back inside the budget. The left end never moves back.
Both ends only ever move right, so every bottle is added once and dropped at most once and the whole scan is linear. Take the best length after each shrink rather than only at the end.
follow_ups: Return the first and last index of one longest certifiable stretch instead of its length. Which one do you return when several tie?

Each bottle now carries a severity from 0 to 3 rather than a flag, and a stretch is certifiable when the severities inside it sum to at most k. Does the same sweep still work, and what exactly changed?
The checks arrive as a stream you cannot re-read, and you must answer after every one. What do you have to keep?

complexity_probe.generator:
def make_input(n):
    # Exactly k failures in the whole run, so the entire line is one legal stretch and a
    # naive per-start rescan reaches the end every time -- O(n^2). Denser failures cut
    # those scans short and hide the defect completely.
    checks = [0] * n
    for i in range(1, 4):
        checks[(i * n) // 4] = 1
    return [checks, 3]

items.title: Largest block a shrink-wrapper can take from an aisle
items.statement_md:
A warehouse aisle has bays in a row, and bay `i` is stacked `heights[i]` units high. Every
unit is the same size and the stacks sit flush against each other.

A shrink-wrapper takes one **rectangular** block at a time: the block spans a run of
consecutive bays and takes the same number of units from every bay in that run, so a block
`h` units high across `w` bays needs all `w` of those bays stacked at least `h` high.

Return the largest number of units one block can hold.

Heights are zero or more and the aisle may be empty.

hints: Fix one bay and ask what the largest block through it looks like. Its height is that bay's height — so the only question left is how wide it can be.
For each bay you want the nearest bay to its left that is shorter than it, and the nearest such bay to its right. Everything strictly between those two is at least as tall.
Sweep left to right keeping a stack of bay indices whose heights increase. A bay shorter than the stack's top is exactly the right bound for that top, so pop it and settle its block.
When you pop, whatever is left on the stack is the left bound, so the width is the gap between the two bounds. Finish by sweeping a bay of height zero past the end so nothing is left unsettled.

The wrapper can now take a block that skips a single bay somewhere in the middle. Does the stack still get you there?

    return [[7] * n]

items.title: Slowest sorter rate that still clears the backlog
items.statement_md:
A depot has a backlog of parcel batches waiting on one sorter, `batches[i]` parcels in the
i-th batch.

The sorter is booked by the hour and works a single batch per hour. At rate `r` it clears up
to `r` parcels from that batch and then stops for the hour — a batch with fewer than `r`
parcels left still uses the whole hour, and the sorter does not move on to another batch
inside it.

A faster rate costs more, so you want the **lowest whole-number rate** that clears the whole
backlog inside `hours` hours.

Return that rate. Return `-1` when no rate is fast enough, and `0` when there is nothing to
sort.

A batch of b parcels at rate r takes the ceiling of b over r hours, not b over r — the leftover parcels still occupy a whole hour of their own.
